nameStory: This little plant gets its name from its love of salty marshes and its tendency to 'spurry' or scatter quickly across sandy, disturbed ground. The 'sand spurry' part comes from how it spreads rapidly in sandy soils, while 'saltmarsh' tells you exactly where to look for it - those brackish areas where land meets sea.
description: Saltmarsh Sand Spurry is a low-growing, sprawling plant that hugs the ground in salty coastal areas. This small annual or sometimes perennial has thin, spreading stems that can reach up to 14 inches long, creating loose mats across the sand and mud. Its tiny white to pink flowers are delicate but numerous, and the whole plant has a rather succulent, fleshy appearance that helps it cope with salt spray and harsh coastal conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pale pink flowers with 5 petals that are shorter than the green sepals behind them, giving flowers a slightly 'overwhelmed' look where the green parts stick out past the petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms sprawling, prostrate mats with stems radiating outward from the center, rarely standing upright but instead hugging the ground like a green carpet

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, fleshy, needle-like leaves that feel slightly succulent when pinched, arranged in clusters along the stems and often with a bluish-green tint

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, triangular seeds contained in papery capsules that split open when ripe, often with a slightly rough texture when rubbed between fingers

habitat: Look for Saltmarsh Sand Spurry in coastal salt marshes, tidal flats, and the edges of salt ponds throughout New England's coastline. It thrives in sandy or muddy soils that are regularly flooded with salt water, often growing alongside glasswort and sea lavender. You might also find it in disturbed saline areas inland, like roadsides that get heavy salt treatment in winter.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin emerging in late spring, with the fleshy leaves and sprawling stems becoming visible as the ground warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from mid-summer through early fall, when the tiny white-pink flowers are most abundant and visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed production and dispersal as the papery capsules split open.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil, though some perennial individuals may persist as small, dormant crowns.

funFact: This tiny plant is essentially a natural desalination expert - it can actually excrete excess salt through special glands on its leaves, sometimes leaving visible white salt crystals on the leaf surfaces that you can taste if you lick them!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other sand spurries, but Saltmarsh Sand Spurry is the only one that thrives in truly salty conditions. If you're in a salt marsh or coastal area, you've probably found the saltmarsh species. The inland sand spurries prefer fresh, non-salty soils.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has caused some confusion - you might see this plant listed as either Spergularia marina or Spergularia salina in different field guides, as botanists have debated the proper classification. Both names refer to its salty habitat preferences.
compareHints: Unlike Red Sand Spurrey which has distinctly pink flowers and grows in dry, non-salty areas, Saltmarsh Sand Spurry has white to very pale pink flowers and requires salty conditions. Canada Sand-spurry is much less common and typically grows in freshwater coastal areas rather than salt marshes, with larger flowers and less fleshy leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red sand spurrey differs from its relative saltmarsh sand spurrey by growing in dry sandy areas rather than salt marshes, and having smaller flowers with less fleshy leaves.
Canada sand-spurry is the most cold-tolerant and northern of the three sand-spurries in New England.
